rows.q: What did the ISACA fabrication look like, according to the quotecheck text?
rows.answer:
According to the quotecheck text, the ISACA fabrication occurred when an agent reading the ISACA CISA Review Manual for the wiki produced, as if it were ISACA's own words, the sentence "a security audit does not typically test information security in an organization but just indicates the extent of compliance with standards." That sentence does not actually appear in the manual. The phrase "indicates the extent of compliance with standards" does exist, but only once, in a different column of a two-column page; because the manual is a 304 MB scanned PDF, running pdftotext -layout welded the two separate columns together line by line, manufacturing a sentence that read plausibly but never existed. The fabrication was especially convincing—and survived earlier checks—because it read like "the compliance profession indicting itself in its own credentialing text," exactly the kind of finding the brief had asked for. It was only caught when all 292 quoted passages across the fifteen CISA pages were machine-checked; the fabricated quote was then removed and the removal recorded on the page.

Sources: /texts/quotecheck

rows.q: Why does Parking II say the number changed from 2 745?
rows.answer:
Parking II says the number moved from 2,745 to 2,263 because the original figure (Text 01, "Prague lost 2 745 stalls") had borrowed car-growth data from a broader European series, with the last three years being an assumption. Parking II replaces that assumption by measuring the fleet directly from Czech vehicle registrations (2010–2022, EEA CO2 monitoring data). Using that measured Czech series in the same fleet and capacity model, the loss comes out to 2,263 stalls (1.33%, with a band of 1,988–2,710) rather than 2,745. As the text puts it, the growth to 2022 survives to the millimetre, but the number does not, because the last three years were an assumption, and an assumption is where the two sources part; Text 01's 2,745 sits just above the top of the new band.

Sources: /texts/prague-parking-2, /texts/prague-parking

rows.q: What is the surfable rule on the surf page?
rows.answer:
The "surfable" rule (version one) on the surf page defines a day as surfable when the daily maximum swell height is between 1.0 and 2.5 m, the mean period is at least 8 s, and the wind is at most 25 km/h or offshore (within east ± 60°). Applied to the last 92 days of analysis at Ericeira, this rule clears five days as surfable.

Sources: /texts/surf

rows.q: What is the Frankl finding in the quotecheck text?
rows.answer:
The Frankl finding: quotecheck's tool was run against the actual extracted text of Man's Search for Meaning and found that the famous quote widely attributed to Viktor Frankl — "Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response" — does not appear in the book. This is a well-known misattribution, and even with the checker deliberately made lenient enough to match another quote (Hardy) through just a page number, it still correctly flagged this Frankl quote as ABSENT, which the text calls "the only test that counts."

Sources: /texts/quotecheck
